Why This Course Opens With a Spec

Software is increasingly written with an AI coding agent's help — the skill that matters is directing it, not typing every line yourself.

Every project you've built in Laravel so far started the same way: open the editor, scaffold a migration, write a controller. This one starts differently — with a document instead of a line of code. That's deliberate, and it's worth explaining why before diving into what the document actually says.

A skill that's quietly becoming as important as writing code is directing code that gets written by something other than you — increasingly, by an AI coding agent. Ask an agent to "build a ticketing system" with nothing more than that sentence, and you'll get something, but not necessarily the something you meant: which fields does a ticket have, does a comment need its own URL, what happens when an assigned agent leaves the team? Left unspecified, an agent fills every one of those gaps with a guess. Some guesses will be wrong, and you won't have a clean way to catch it early or steer the work back on course, because there was never anything concrete to check the output against in the first place.

An architecture brief — what a system is, what it's made of, and why it's shaped the way it is, written down before any code exists — is the tool that closes that gap. It gives an agent something concrete to build against. It gives you something concrete to check the result against, question by question, before a single line is wrong in a way that's expensive to unwind. And it gives whoever reads the code afterwards — a teammate, a reviewer, future-you in six weeks — a fast way back into why something looks the way it does, without archaeology through commit history.

That's what this page is: the brief for the system you're about to build, lesson by lesson, for the rest of this course. It isn't a one-off exercise either. Real engineering teams increasingly keep a document exactly like this one in the repository itself — partly because it's useful on its own, and partly because it turns out to be the natural interface for directing an AI agent's work: something to hand it before it starts, something to check its output against once it's done, something both a human reviewer and the agent's next session can re-read to pick up where things left off. The codebase you're about to build was itself built against a document that plays exactly that role.
